title: Organizations the City pays that pay lobbyists
question: Is public money paying to lobby for more of it?
finding: 86 lobbying clients are nonprofits the City funds or payees of $1 million or more since fiscal 2019; lobbyists reported $14.0 million from them, $3.1 million of it from 30 City-funded nonprofits. 681 of their reported contacts mention a contract, grant, lease, budget or funding. The largest payers among the nonprofits: California Pacific Medical Center ($870,340), Exploratorium ($337,500), Corporation of Fine Arts Museums ($255,000).
how: Clients in the lobbyist reports are matched by name to the City payment ledger (fiscal 2019 to 2026) and to this project’s profiles of City-funded nonprofits. A contact is “about money” when its subject, issue or outcome sought mentions a contract, grant, lease, award, budget, appropriation, funding or purchase. This extends the paid-clients table in the “lobby triangle” results with fees, firms and the nonprofits.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. A nonprofit may spend private donations, not City money, on a lobbyist; the reports do not say which money paid the fee. Many of these clients are large companies or hospitals for which City payments are a small part of their business, and their contacts are often about permits or rules, not their contracts. A name match can join two different bodies.
